findings.issue_text: Backup codes in next-auth-options.ts are stored reversibly encrypted with the same key as the TOTP secret instead of salted-hashed, so anyone with DB read plus the key can recover all valid codes
Once all backup codes are consumed the array becomes all nulls but the MissingBackupCodes check only tests !user.backupCodes, so login attempts silently return IncorrectBackupCode
Backup-code login path in next-auth-options.ts skips the checkRateLimitAndThrowError rate limiting applied to TOTP, allowing brute force of 40-bit codes
disable.ts backup-code path bypasses TOTP check, has no rate limiting, and accepts a backup code alone to disable 2FA, allowing a session holder to brute-force codes and strip 2FA
Read-modify-write of backupCodes array in next-auth-options.ts is not atomic; concurrent logins with the same code can both pass indexOf, allowing a single-use code to be used twice
setup.ts generates and persists backup codes before TOTP is confirmed (twoFactorEnabled: false) and returns them in the response, so users can download codes for a 2FA that never activated
formatBackupCode in EnableTwoFactorModal.tsx is a const arrow declared after handleSetup but referenced inside it, creating a TDZ trap for any synchronous use
URL.revokeObjectURL in EnableTwoFactorModal.tsx uses stale closure state and the object URL is never revoked on unmount or after download, leaking a Blob per setup attempt
The <a download> wrapping a <Button> inside a <Form> in EnableTwoFactorModal.tsx renders a button defaulting to type=submit, so clicking Download may also submit the enable form
Close button on the backup-codes step in EnableTwoFactorModal.tsx calls resetState() but does not clear backupCodes, backupCodesUrl, dataUri, or secret, exposing previous secret/codes on reopen

In EnableTwoFactorModal.tsx, onOpenChange (overlay click / Esc) closes the dialog on the backup-codes step without calling onEnable(), so the 2FA switch never flips and codes are lost with no way to view them again
BackupCode.tsx component is exported as TwoFactor instead of BackupCode, mislabeling stack traces/devtools and colliding with the real TwoFactor

In DisableTwoFactorModal, react-hook-form keeps the unmounted backupCode/totpCode field registered when twoFactorLostAccess toggles, so a stale non-empty backup code is silently preferred over the TOTP code the user just typed
JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(...)) is uncaught in disable.ts and next-auth-options.ts, so a corrupt or re-keyed backupCodes value throws and returns a 500
String.prototype.replaceAll in disable.ts requires Node 15+ / ES2021 lib and may fail typecheck if the tsconfig target/lib is lower
disable.ts enters the backup code path whenever req.body.backupCode is truthy without a type check, so a non-string body value reaches .replaceAll and throws a 500; should validate with zod
No e2e test in login.2fa.e2e.ts covers logging in with a backup code, single-use enforcement, or disabling 2FA via backup code
FIXME in login.2fa.e2e.ts leaves a no-op assertion (expect(locator.isChecked()).toBeTruthy()) asserting on a Promise instead of fixing it to await expect(locator).toBeChecked()
login.tsx renders BackupCode but formSchema (zod resolver) may not include backupCode, so submissions with the backup field could fail validation; verify formSchema was updated

goldens.comment: The exported function TwoFactor handles backup codes and is in BackupCode.tsx. Inconsistent naming.
Error message mentions 'backup code login' but this is a disable endpoint, not login

Backup code validation is case-sensitive due to the use of indexOf(). This causes validation to fail if a user enters uppercase hex characters, as backup codes should be case-insensitive for a better user experience.

Because backupCodes are decrypted and mutated in memory before being written back, two concurrent login requests using the same backupCode could both pass this check and update, so a single backup code may effectively be accepted more than once if used concurrently, weakening the intended one-time-use semantics.

Object URL for backup codes is not revoked on component unmount, leading to a potential memory leak. This can cause increased memory usage over time, especially if the component is mounted and unmounted frequently.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Backup codes in next-auth-options.ts are stored reversibly encrypted with the same key as the TOTP secret instead of salted-hashed, so anyone with DB read plus the key can recover all valid codes

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces `backupCodes` stored in the `users` table as `TEXT` and populated via `symmetricEncrypt(JSON.stringify(backupCodes), process.env.CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY)` in `totp/setup.ts`. In `next-auth-options.ts` and the disable API, those codes are later recovered with `symmetricDecrypt(..., process.env.CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY)` and compared in plaintext (`indexOf(credentials.backupCode.replaceAll("-", ""))`). This is reversible encryption using the same shared application key used to encrypt the TOTP secret, not salted hashing. Therefore, anyone with DB read access plus the encryption key can decrypt and recover the remaining valid backup codes.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Once all backup codes are consumed the array becomes all nulls but the MissingBackupCodes check only tests !user.backupCodes, so login attempts silently return IncorrectBackupCode

adjudication.rationale: In `next-auth-options.ts`, backup codes are stored as an encrypted JSON array string (`user.backupCodes`). When a backup code is successfully used, the code sets that entry to `null` and re-encrypts the array (`backupCodes[index] = null; ... backupCodes: symmetricEncrypt(JSON.stringify(backupCodes), ...)`). If all codes are consumed, the decrypted array will be `[null, null, ...]` but `user.backupCodes` is still a non-empty string, so the `if (!user.backupCodes) throw MissingBackupCodes;` check will not trigger. Subsequent login attempts with any backup code will fail the `indexOf(...)` lookup and throw `IncorrectBackupCode` rather than `MissingBackupCodes` (i.e., the code can’t distinguish “no codes left” from “wrong code”).

adjudication_records.issue_text: Backup-code login path in next-auth-options.ts skips the checkRateLimitAndThrowError rate limiting applied to TOTP, allowing brute force of 40-bit codes

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a new `if (user.twoFactorEnabled && credentials.backupCode)` branch in `next-auth-options.ts`, but the shown hunks do not include any `checkRateLimitAndThrowError(...)` calls for either the TOTP path or the new backup-code path. Since the location/scope of existing rate limiting is not visible in the diff, it is not verifiable from this change that backup-code login “skips” rate limiting that TOTP has. The claim depends on unseen surrounding code.

formatBackupCode in EnableTwoFactorModal.tsx is a const arrow declared after handleSetup but referenced inside it, creating a TDZ trap for any synchronous use

adjudication.rationale: In EnableTwoFactorModal.tsx, handleSetup references formatBackupCode, which is declared later as a const arrow. While const declarations have a TDZ during *module/component execution*, handleSetup is only *defined* before formatBackupCode, not executed. The function body won’t run until a user submits the form, by which time the component function has finished executing and formatBackupCode has been initialized for that render. There is no synchronous invocation of handleSetup during the TDZ window shown in the diff, so this is not a real, verifiable bug.

adjudication_records.issue_text: The <a download> wrapping a <Button> inside a <Form> in EnableTwoFactorModal.tsx renders a button defaulting to type=submit, so clicking Download may also submit the enable form

adjudication.rationale: Not verifiable from the diff. The claim depends on how the shared <Button> component is implemented (whether it renders a native <button> with implicit type="submit" vs defaulting to type="button"). The diff does not show Button’s implementation, and the file already contains multiple <Button> usages inside a <Form> without an explicit type (e.g., cancel/close/copy), which would already be problematic if Button defaulted to submit. This strongly suggests Button likely defaults to type="button", making the finding speculative rather than a demonstrated defect in this diff.

In EnableTwoFactorModal.tsx, onOpenChange (overlay click / Esc) closes the dialog on the backup-codes step without calling onEnable(), so the 2FA switch never flips and codes are lost with no way to view them again

adjudication.rationale: The diff changes the success path of enabling 2FA: in EnableTwoFactorModal.handleEnable, a 200 response now does `setStep(SetupStep.DisplayBackupCodes)` instead of calling `onEnable()`. The only place `onEnable()` is called now is the "close" button in the DisplayBackupCodes step (`backup-codes-close`). However, the Dialog is still rendered as `<Dialog open={open} onOpenChange={onOpenChange}>` with no special handling during the backup-codes step, so overlay click / Esc can trigger `onOpenChange` and close the dialog without executing the "close" button handler. In that case this component will not call `onEnable()` (nor `resetState()`), meaning any parent-side "2FA enabled" refresh/toggle logic tied to `onEnable()` will be skipped, and the user can miss the one-time display of backup codes (this UI has no other code path to show them again).

adjudication_records.issue_text: In DisableTwoFactorModal, react-hook-form keeps the unmounted backupCode/totpCode field registered when twoFactorLostAccess toggles, so a stale non-empty backup code is silently preferred over the TOTP code the user just typed
JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(...)) is uncaught in disable.ts and next-auth-options.ts, so a corrupt or re-keyed backupCodes value throws and returns a 500

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces `JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(...))` in both `apps/web/pages/api/auth/two-factor/totp/disable.ts` and `packages/features/auth/lib/next-auth-options.ts` without any local try/catch or validation. If `user.backupCodes` is corrupted or the encryption key changes (so decryption yields non-JSON), `JSON.parse` will throw. In `disable.ts` that would bubble out of the handler (typically resulting in a 500), and in `authorize` it would throw out of NextAuth auth flow (also resulting in an internal error rather than a controlled `ErrorCode`). This is a concrete robustness/correctness issue introduced by the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: String.prototype.replaceAll in disable.ts requires Node 15+ / ES2021 lib and may fail typecheck if the tsconfig target/lib is lower

adjudication.rationale: The diff does introduce new uses of `String.prototype.replaceAll` (e.g. in `apps/web/pages/api/auth/two-factor/totp/disable.ts` and `packages/features/auth/lib/next-auth-options.ts`). However, the proposed finding claims it will fail due to Node/runtime or TS `lib` settings being too low, which is not verifiable from the diff (no Node version/tsconfig changes shown, and the repo may already target ES2021+ or already use `replaceAll`). This is a conditional concern rather than a concrete defect demonstrated by the patch.

adjudication_records.issue_text: disable.ts enters the backup code path whenever req.body.backupCode is truthy without a type check, so a non-string body value reaches .replaceAll and throws a 500; should validate with zod

adjudication.rationale: In `apps/web/pages/api/auth/two-factor/totp/disable.ts`, the new branch `if (user.twoFactorEnabled && req.body.backupCode)` only checks truthiness. It then calls `req.body.backupCode.replaceAll("-", "")`. If a client sends a JSON body where `backupCode` is a non-string truthy value (e.g., `{}`, `[]`, `1`, `true`), `replaceAll` will be undefined and throw a `TypeError`, resulting in a 500 instead of a controlled 4xx error. There is no runtime type validation in this handler, so this is a real defect introduced by the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: No e2e test in login.2fa.e2e.ts covers logging in with a backup code, single-use enforcement, or disabling 2FA via backup code

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds backup-code functionality to login and 2FA disable flows, but `apps/web/playwright/login.2fa.e2e.ts` only adds checks around displaying/downloading/copying backup codes after enabling 2FA. It even contains a `// TODO: add more backup code tests, e.g. login + disabling 2fa with backup` comment, and there is no test that logs in using `backupCode`, verifies single-use behavior, or disables 2FA via backup code.

adjudication_records.issue_text: FIXME in login.2fa.e2e.ts leaves a no-op assertion (expect(locator.isChecked()).toBeTruthy()) asserting on a Promise instead of fixing it to await expect(locator).toBeChecked()

adjudication.rationale: In apps/web/playwright/login.2fa.e2e.ts the test does `await expect(page.locator('[data-testid=two-factor-switch]').isChecked()).toBeTruthy();`. `locator.isChecked()` returns a Promise<boolean>, and without awaiting it this assertion checks the truthiness of the Promise object (always truthy), making the check effectively a no-op. A correct check would be `await expect(locator).toBeChecked()` or `expect(await locator.isChecked()).toBeTruthy()`.

adjudication_records.issue_text: login.tsx renders BackupCode but formSchema (zod resolver) may not include backupCode, so submissions with the backup field could fail validation; verify formSchema was updated

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows `login.tsx` adding a `backupCode` field to `LoginValues` and conditionally rendering `<BackupCode />`, while still using `zodResolver(formSchema)`. However, the actual `formSchema` definition is not included anywhere in the provided diff, so we cannot confirm whether it was updated to include `backupCode` (or whether it’s permissive via `.passthrough()` etc.). The finding is therefore speculative rather than a verifiable defect in the diff itself.
